summary:
Codyseey is an open-source, interactive 3D WebGL lunar exploration browser built for NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative and Artemis program.

Addressing Challenge 4: CLPS Lunar Mission Browser, Codyseey integrates real NASA LRO LOLA elevation grids, LROC photographic basemaps, and JPL DE441 planetary ephemerides into a zero-install, real-time simulation. Users can inspect candidate South Pole landing sites (including Malapert Mountain and Nobile Crater), simulate powered descent, drive rovers (NASA VIPER and Griffin Rover 2) with physical 6-wheel terrain contact, and execute TRIDENT subsurface drill assays for volatile water-ice deposits.

The lunar South Pole presents extreme operational hazards sub-degree solar grazing angles, prolonged night occultations, and cryogenic Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs). Codyseey replaces weeks of manual ephemeris scripting with an intuitive, multi-track synodic timeline (2026–2030), instantly calculating direct solar illumination corridors and Earth communications links. It democratizes mission planning for engineers, researchers, and students worldwide.
details:
1. What Exactly Does It Do?

Codyseey is an open-source, zero-install, 3D lunar mission planning and ephemeris exploration platform built specifically for NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative and the Artemis campaign. It bridges the gap between raw planetary science datasets and actionable mission operations, allowing planners, scientists, and students to:

  • Explore Candidate Landing Sites: Inspect high-priority South Pole landing havens—such as Malapert Mountain, Shackleton Connecting Ridge, Mons Mouton, and Nobile Crater Rim—with authentic lunar topology.
  • Simulate Surface Operations: Drive robotic rovers (NASA VIPER and Astrobotic Griffin Rover 2) featuring dynamic 6-wheel rocker-bogie terrain contact physics, slope-hazard detection, and hazard-cam telemetry.
  • Execute Volatile Prospecting: Deploy the 1-meter TRIDENT rotary-percussive drill to simulate subsurface core sample extraction and geochemical volatile assays in Permanently Shadowed Regions (PSRs).
  • Track Synodic Sun & Earth Corridors (2026–2030): Calculate real-time line-of-sight communications with Earth and sub-degree solar illumination angles to ensure mission survival.

2. How Does It Work?

Codyseey runs entirely in the browser using a client-side, hardware-accelerated WebGL engine built on Three.js:

  1. Topographic Altimetry Pipeline: Integrates real elevation data from the Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter (LOLA) onboard NASA’s Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter (LRO). The surface engine computes per-vertex heightfields and terrain normals to accurately render micro-craters, boulder fields, and ridge slopes.
  2. Planetary Ephemeris Engine: Ingests high-precision vectors derived from NASA JPL DE441 Planetary Ephemerides and NASA SPICE kernels. It computes the precise 3D vector positions of the Sun and Earth relative to the lunar South Pole across the entire synodic cycle from 2026 through 2030.
  3. Terrain & Wheel Contact Physics: Uses mathematical ground-plane contact constraints combined with rocker-bogie suspension articulation. As the rover navigates, each wheel independently tracks local elevation gradients, ensuring realistic physical interaction without floating or clipping into the regolith.
  4. High-Fidelity PBR Shader Engine: Utilizes physically-based rendering (PBR) calibrated with authentic Apollo 17 lunar sample specs (Sample 70017 vesicular basalt). Shaders dynamically account for zero-atmosphere direct solar glare, high-contrast harsh shadows, and subtle earthshine fill.

3. What Tools, Technologies & NASA Data Were Used?

  • Frontend & Core Engine: React 18, Vite, Three.js (r160+), WebGL 2.0.
  • Physics & Mathematical Modeling: Custom 6-wheel rocker-bogie suspension solver, raycasting collision detection, and spline-based traverse interpolation.
    • LRO LOLA: Global and polar DEMs (Digital Elevation Models) for elevation, slope hazard grading, and crater mapping.
    • LRO LROC (WAC & NAC): Global color basemaps and high-resolution Narrow Angle Camera imagery.
    • NASA JPL DE441: Ephemeris data providing exact Sun and Earth positions, sub-solar latitudes, and synodic luncation cycles.
    • Apollo 17 Station 6 Geochemistry: Vesicular basalt morphology and regolith albedo standards.

4. What Factors Did Our Team Consider & How Is It Creative?

  • The Harsh Reality of the Lunar South Pole: Unlike equatorial regions, South Pole solar grazing angles hover between 1.5° and −1.5°, casting immense, dynamic shadows. A rover that drives into a Permanently Shadowed Region (PSR) risks sudden battery freeze-out and cryogenic death at 40 Kelvin. Codyseey directly addresses this by providing instant line-of-sight solar and communications tracking.
  • Collapsible Minimalist Timeline: Designed a sleek, single-line collapsible synodic timeline (2026–2030) with faded gradient ends and an interactive Earth/Sun tracking bead, giving users both high-level overview and minute-by-minute tactical planning.
  • Zero-Barrier Accessibility: Rather than locking planetary mission planning behind specialized command-line scripts or proprietary GIS software, Codyseey packages full PBR physics into a lightweight, responsive web app that runs seamlessly on any standard laptop or desktop browser.

5. Intended Impact & Benefits

  • Accelerating CLPS Mission Trajectories: Enables commercial lander operators and science teams to prototype traverse routes and identify continuous sunlight survival corridors in seconds rather than weeks.
  • Risk Mitigation: Visualizes line-of-sight occultations to prevent catastrophic loss of signal (LOS) with NASA's Deep Space Network (DSN).
  • STEM Democratization: Empowers researchers, university students, and space enthusiasts worldwide with interactive access to authentic NASA planetary science.
